The Finite Element Method

11 May 2026 · Download PDF · Download code

Contents
  1. 1. Getting the computer to understand functions
  2. 2. The Finite Element Method for the Helmholtz equation

The aim of the Finite Element Method (FEM) is to solve (or more precisely approximate the solution of) a Partial Differential Equation (PDE) using a computer. In general the solution to a PDE is a function. Unfortunately it is computationally intractable to task a computer with finding this underlying function. The idea to resolve this issue is to parametrize a family of functions with the aim of computing the parameters through solving a linear system of equations. There is a plethora of ways to get to such a linear system of equations, with the most common being the so-called Galerkin approach.

1. Getting the computer to understand functions

In the most basic terms, computers are only capable of understanding numbers, which means that they are inherently unable to solve equations where the unknowns are functions. This is a problem when trying to solve differential equations. To solve this problem, the functions are instead approximated using parameterizations for which the coefficients (numbers) are unknown. Intuitively, these numbers are exactly what the computer is asked to find. For element methods, this parameterization is chosen to be the simplest possible: a linear combination of functions

𝑝(𝐱)≈𝐓(𝐱)𝐩=[𝑇1(𝐱)𝑇2(𝐱)…𝑇𝑛(𝐱)][𝑝1𝑝2⋮𝑝𝑛],

(1)

where 𝑝 is the unknown function being approximated. Note that the linearity is with respect to the unknown parameters 𝐩, but not necessarily in the known basis functions 𝐓(𝐱).

One might ask: How does the above relate to the Finite Element Method? The answer is that the functions 𝑇𝑖 are chosen to be simpler functions with support equal to only a few subdomains of the original domain. These subdomains are commonly referred to as elements.

2. The Finite Element Method for the Helmholtz equation

In acoustics we are often interested in solving the Helmholtz equation, given as

Δ𝑝(𝐱)+𝑘2𝑝(𝐱)=0,𝐱∈Ω,

(2)

where 𝑘 is most often referred to as the wavenumber. In its current form the basis functions 𝐓(𝐱) must be twice differentiable; piecewise linear functions, for example, have a vanishing second derivative inside each element and cannot be used. This constraint can be relieved using the so-called weak formulation. In order to do so we multiply the Helmholtz equation with a so-called test function 𝜑 followed by an integration over the domain Ω

∫Ω𝜑(𝐱)(Δ𝑝(𝐱)+𝑘2𝑝(𝐱))d𝐱=0.

(3)

Utilizing integration by parts on the term including the Laplacian we can move derivatives from 𝑝(𝐱) onto 𝜑(𝐱) as

∫Ω(∇𝜑(𝐱))⊤∇𝑝(𝐱)d𝐱−𝑘2∫Ω𝜑(𝐱)𝑝(𝐱)d𝐱−∫𝜕Ω𝜑(𝐱)𝜕𝑝𝜕𝑛(𝐱)d𝐱=0.

(4)

In the above the constraint on the smoothness of 𝑝(𝐱) has been reduced to first order. Furthermore the last term

∫𝜕Ω𝜑(𝐱)𝜕𝑝𝜕𝑛(𝐱)d𝐱

(5)

can be used to include the boundary conditions into the equation. For simplification purposes we will in the following assume that the above is equal to zero. As such we have

0=∫Ω(∇𝜑(𝐱))⊤∇𝑝(𝐱)d𝐱−𝑘2∫Ω𝜑(𝐱)𝑝(𝐱)d𝐱.

(6)

We will now use the Galerkin approach to discretize the above equation. Note that “Galerkin” simply refers to the approach where 𝜑(𝐱) and 𝑝(𝐱) are discretized using the same basis functions (𝐓(𝐱)). In short this means that we introduce

𝑝(𝐱)≈𝐓(𝐱)𝐩,𝜑(𝐱)≈𝐚⊤𝐓(𝐱)⊤,

(7)

where 𝐚∈ℂ𝑛 is a set of arbitrary coefficients that parametrize a whole family of test functions and 𝐩∈ℂ𝑛 are the coefficients that we aim to find. Inserting the approximations it follows that

0=∫Ω(∇𝜑(𝐱))⊤∇𝑝(𝐱)d𝐱−𝑘2∫Ω𝜑(𝐱)𝑝(𝐱)d𝐱≈∫Ω𝐚⊤(∇𝐓(𝐱))⊤∇𝐓(𝐱)𝐩d𝐱−𝑘2∫Ω𝐚⊤𝐓(𝐱)⊤𝐓(𝐱)𝐩d𝐱=𝐚⊤(∫Ω(∇𝐓(𝐱))⊤∇𝐓(𝐱)d𝐱)𝐩−𝑘2𝐚⊤(∫Ω𝐓(𝐱)⊤𝐓(𝐱)d𝐱)𝐩=𝐚⊤(∫Ω(∇𝐓(𝐱))⊤∇𝐓(𝐱)d𝐱−𝑘2∫Ω𝐓(𝐱)⊤𝐓(𝐱)d𝐱)𝐩.

(8)

We can make the above equality hold for all possible test functions, i.e. for all 𝐚∈ℂ𝑛, if we find 𝐩 such that

(∫Ω(∇𝐓(𝐱))⊤∇𝐓(𝐱)d𝐱−𝑘2∫Ω𝐓(𝐱)⊤𝐓(𝐱)d𝐱)𝐩=𝟎.

(9)

This is exactly what we do in Finite Element computations. As a shorthand the above can be written as

(𝐊−𝑘2𝐌)𝐩=𝟎,

(10)

where 𝐊 is referred to as the stiffness matrix and 𝐌 as the mass matrix. In the literature the equation can also be found as

(𝑐2𝐊−𝜔2𝐌)𝐩=𝟎,

(11)

where 𝑐 is the propagation speed and 𝜔 is the angular frequency.

3. What is an element?

A key insight is that the element serves two purposes: it represents a subdomain of the original domain (also referred to as the geometry) while also describing parts of the unknown function(s) of interest. In general this subdomain is described by a parameterization, i.e. the element, as

𝐱𝑒(𝐮)=𝐗𝑒𝐍𝑒(𝐮)∈Ω𝑒,∀𝐮∈ℒ︀𝑒,

(12)

where the superscript 𝑒 denotes the element number, 𝐗𝑒 is a matrix with columns equal to the interpolation nodes of the geometry, 𝐍𝑒(𝐮) are the so-called shape functions, Ω𝑒 is the element in global coordinates and ℒ︀𝑒 are the local coordinates. In addition to the geometric interpolation of each element, we need to further define interpolations of the unknown functions, which in acoustics is usually taken as the pressure 𝑝(𝐱). On element 𝑒 this interpolation can be done as

𝑝(𝐱𝑒(𝐮))=𝐓(𝐱𝑒(𝐮))𝐩=𝐓(𝐱𝑒(𝐮))(𝐋𝑒)⊤⏟𝐓𝑒(𝐮)𝐋𝑒𝐩⏟𝐩𝑒=𝐓𝑒(𝐮)𝐩𝑒,𝐮∈ℒ︀𝑒,

(13)

where 𝐋𝑒 is a permutation-like matrix that extracts the relevant values of 𝐩 and the relevant functions of 𝐓(𝐱) and orders them such that they correspond to the local values 𝐩𝑒 and the local basis functions 𝐓𝑒(𝐮).

4. Computing the stiffness and mass matrices

Using the element description of both the geometry and the pressure function the mass matrix can be computed as follows

𝐌=∫Ω𝐓(𝐱)⊤𝐓(𝐱)d𝐱≈∑𝑒=1𝑁∫Ω𝑒𝐋𝑒⊤𝐋𝑒𝐓(𝐱)⊤𝐓(𝐱)𝐋𝑒⊤𝐋𝑒d𝐱=∑𝑒=1𝑁𝐋𝑒⊤(∫ℒ︀𝑒𝐓𝑒(𝐮)⊤𝐓𝑒(𝐮)jacobian(Ω𝑒,𝐮)d𝐮)𝐋𝑒≈∑𝑒=1𝑁𝐋𝑒⊤(∑𝑖=1𝑄𝑤𝑖𝐓𝑒(𝐮𝑖)⊤𝐓𝑒(𝐮𝑖)jacobian(Ω𝑒,𝐮𝑖)⏟𝐌𝑒)𝐋𝑒,

(18)

where the first approximation is due to the geometry being approximated by the elements, and the second is due to the quadrature with the 𝑄 points 𝐮𝑖 and weights 𝑤𝑖. Furthermore, jacobian(Ω𝑒,𝐮) is a function that describes the distortion from the local coordinates ℒ︀𝑒 onto the global element Ω𝑒. This distortion represents length, area, or volume depending on the dimensionality of the problem. Note that if the elements are the same size then 𝐌𝑒 is constant with respect to each element (this is the case in the code below).

The stiffness matrix is computed similarly but with a difference in the fact that the gradient must have its coordinates changed from global to local. Using the chain rule it follows that

∇𝐮𝑝(𝐱(𝐮))=𝐉(𝐮)∇𝐱𝑝(𝐱(𝐮)),

(19)

where 𝐉(𝐮)=(𝜕𝐱/𝜕𝐮)⊤, i.e. 𝐽𝑖𝑗=(𝜕𝑥𝑗)/(𝜕𝑢𝑖), so that jacobian(Ω𝑒,𝐮)=|det𝐉(𝐮)|. From this we can isolate the global gradient as

∇𝐱𝑝(𝐱(𝐮))=𝐉(𝐮)−1∇𝐮𝑝(𝐱(𝐮)).

(20)

Putting things together the stiffness matrix can therefore be computed as

𝐊=∫Ω(∇𝐓(𝐱))⊤∇𝐓(𝐱)d𝐱≈∑𝑒=1𝑁∫Ω𝑒𝐋𝑒⊤𝐋𝑒(∇𝐱𝐓(𝐱))⊤∇𝐱𝐓(𝐱)𝐋𝑒⊤𝐋𝑒d𝐱=∑𝑒=1𝑁𝐋𝑒⊤(∫ℒ︀𝑒(∇𝐱𝐓𝑒(𝐮))⊤∇𝐱𝐓𝑒(𝐮)jacobian(Ω𝑒,𝐮)d𝐮)𝐋𝑒=∑𝑒=1𝑁𝐋𝑒⊤(∫ℒ︀𝑒(∇𝐮𝐓𝑒(𝐮))⊤(𝐉(𝐮)⊤)−1𝐉(𝐮)−1∇𝐮𝐓𝑒(𝐮)jacobian(Ω𝑒,𝐮)d𝐮)𝐋𝑒≈∑𝑒=1𝑁𝐋𝑒⊤(∑𝑖=1𝑄𝑤𝑖(∇𝐮𝐓𝑒(𝐮𝑖))⊤(𝐉(𝐮𝑖)⊤)−1𝐉(𝐮𝑖)−1∇𝐮𝐓𝑒(𝐮𝑖)jacobian(Ω𝑒,𝐮𝑖)⏟𝐊𝑒)𝐋𝑒.

(21)
